measurement.happened:
THE EBOLA OUTBREAK DOMINATES EVERYTHING. The single biggest story of the week in DR Congo is the Ebola outbreak, now the second deadliest in history. By the end of the week, cases had surpassed 10,000 and deaths had passed 5,000. Reuters, AP, BBC, AFP, CNN, Deutsche Welle, Bloomberg, and Al Jazeera all reported on this. The UN described the outbreak as growing exponentially. Cases were confirmed outside Congo for the first time: Kenya and Nigeria, with genome sequencing linking those cases back to the Congo chain (Bloomberg, Deutsche Welle). Uganda imposed a 21-day quarantine on its own citizens returning from Congo, and required them to pay for it (Reuters, AP, Al Jazeera). The Central African Republic strengthened border controls (TV5Monde). On the ground, violence against health responders escalated: a nurse was killed and another health worker severely injured by attackers in eastern Congo (Reuters, AP, BBC, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde). A machete-wielding mob attacked health workers responding to an Ebola case (Reuters). Community mistrust is deep: a village chief who lost relatives to Ebola is trying to fight the prejudice against the sick (AP, twice). On a small positive note, CNN and Al Jazeera reported celebrations as the last patients were discharged from one Ebola treatment centre, and a three-shot vaccine trial began in Congo (Bloomberg). The outbreak is straining the health system and feeding fear of a continent-wide spread.

US SANCTIONS ON RWANDA OVER THE EASTERN CONGO CONFLICT. The United States imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry, and also on the Zigama CSS bank, for fueling the M23 rebel conflict in eastern Congo (Reuters, AP, BBC multiple times, Bloomberg, WSJ, TV5Monde). This is a significant escalation in Washington's posture toward Kigali, even though peace agreements had been signed between Congo and Rwanda. TV5Monde asked why Washington is hardening its tone despite those accords. The sanctions target the military machinery rather than the civilian government, which is a deliberate signal. Rwanda's defence ministry is now effectively sanctioned, which will complicate its procurement and banking for a while.

JOSEPH KABILA AND THE FRN REBEL MOVEMENT. BBC reported that former president Joseph Kabila has become DR Congo's latest rebel leader, tied to the FRN (Forces Républicaines Nationales). Tshisekedi publicly called Kabila a supplétif, meaning a puppet or supplement of Rwanda (TV5Monde, BBC in Kinyarwanda). A Brigadier General, François Kamanzi, left the FARDC to join the FRN (BBC, Kinyarwanda). Tensions are building around Uvira, where residents fear a new rebel offensive (TV5Monde video). This is a major political-military development: a former president leading an armed opposition faction changes the character of the conflict from a proxy war into something more like a civil war with a recognizable face.

GOLD SMUGGLING AND THE IS-LINKED ADF INSURGENCY. A Sentry report found that gold smuggling through Uganda is financing the Islamic State-linked ADF insurgency in eastern Congo (Reuters, Bloomberg). The ADF was also accused of banditry in gold mining areas (BBC, Kinyarwanda). This links the mining sector, the cross-border trade routes, and the insurgency in a way that makes the conflict harder to untangle.

ARTISANAL MINING CRACKDOWN AND THE CHINA QUESTION. Congo suspended the head of its artisanal mining regulatory agency for failing to prevent illegal activities (Reuters, Bloomberg). Separately, a Gates-backed mining company said China is frustrating exploration efforts in DR Congo (FT). This suggests the government is trying to tighten control over the sector that funds much of the eastern conflict, while also navigating a complicated relationship with Chinese mining interests.

FATF GREY LIST REMOVAL. The Financial Action Task Force removed DR Congo from its grey list along with Bulgaria, Ivory Coast, and Monaco (Reuters, Bloomberg). This is a positive signal for the country's financial standing and should ease some of the compliance burden on Congolese banks and businesses. It is a small but meaningful win for the government's credibility with international finance.

OPPOSITION AND THE REFERENDUM LAW. The C64 opposition platform met in Rome to coordinate (TV5Monde video). The opposition rejected an armed rebellion and called for inclusive dialogue (Reuters). Meanwhile, a controversial referendum law was adopted in parliament without opposition participation, sparking a firestorm (TV5Monde, two headlines). The opposition sees this as a power grab by Tshisekedi's camp, and the absence of the C64 bloc in the chamber makes the law's legitimacy an open question.

TSHISEKEDI AND FIFA. Tshisekedi publicly showed support for FIFA president Gianni Infantino, with exclusive images of the two together (TV5Monde). This is a soft-power play and hints at possible ambitions around hosting a major football event, though it is a minor story compared to the rest.

A MINOR NOTE. British explorer Ash Dykes completed a Congo Basin expedition after going missing for 24 hours (BBC, twice). Not a headline for long, but it shows the country still draws adventurers and that the interior remains a place where people can vanish.
measurement.expected:
EBOLA (confidence: almost certain to remain the dominant story). Cases and deaths will almost certainly continue to climb in the coming week. The UN's 'growing exponentially' language, the confirmation of cases in Kenya and Nigeria, and the attacks on health workers all point to acceleration, not deceleration. Expect the death toll to cross 6,000 or 7,000 by the end of next week. More neighbouring countries will likely tighten border controls or announce their own cases. The vaccine trial will be in early stages, so no results yet. Community resistance to burial protocols and health workers will remain a flashpoint, and at least one more attack on a medical team is probable. The one small silver lining is that individual treatment centres may continue to discharge patients, giving occasional pockets of relief in the coverage. I am almost certain Ebola will be the top story in every major outlet next week.

RWANDA-CONGO TENSIONS AND KABILA/FRN (confidence: probable to escalate rhetorically, possible for a new military move). The US sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry will almost certainly provoke a response from Kigali, whether a verbal pushback, a reciprocal measure, or a diplomatic note through the AU. Tshisekedi will likely keep calling Kabila a Rwandan puppet, and Kabila's camp will respond. The tension around Uvira and the threat of a new FRN offensive make a new round of fighting in the next week probable, though a full-scale offensive is more possible than certain. The departure of Brig Gen Kamanzi to the FRN will be cited by both sides. I would say a new battle or skirmish in the east is probable, a major offensive is possible, and a ceasefire or truce is unlikely.

OPPOSITION AND REFERENDUM LAW (confidence: probable friction). The C64 platform's Rome meeting will likely produce a joint statement or a set of demands. The opposition's rejection of armed rebellion and call for dialogue will keep them on the diplomatic track, but the referendum law adopted without them will fuel protests or at least street demonstrations in Kinshasa and other cities. I would rate a visible protest or two as probable, a general strike as possible, and a constitutional crisis as unlikely in this short window.

GOLD / MINING / ADF (confidence: possible continued disruption). The suspension of the artisanal mining agency head will likely lead to a replacement appointment within the week, and the new head will face immediate pressure to show results. The Sentry report on gold smuggling funding the ADF will keep the sector in the news. Expect some government announcements about inspections or new rules. A major crackdown or a new smuggling route being exposed is possible.

FATF AND FINANCE (confidence: almost certain to be a footnote). The grey-list removal is done; next week it will mostly be mentioned in passing as context. Banks will quietly adjust compliance procedures. No major financial headline is expected, but the removal may be cited in investment pitches.

CHINA MINING RELATIONS (confidence: possible friction). The Gates-backed company's complaint about China will likely draw a response from Chinese mining interests or from the Congolese government. This is a slow-burn issue and I would not expect a dramatic confrontation next week, but it will keep simmering in trade and mining press.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES (possible but I would not build a forecast around them): a new Ebola case confirmed in a third or fourth country (Tanzania, South Sudan, or the DRC's own southern provinces); a surprise meeting between Tshisekedi and Kabila mediated by the AU or the Church; a new US or EU sanctions package aimed at Congolese officials rather than Rwandan ones; a coup attempt or a cabinet reshuffle triggered by the Ebola crisis; the ADF launching a major attack on a mining site and releasing a video.

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON: a full-scale civil war declaration by Kabila's FRN in this specific week (it is more of a slow escalation); a complete halt to the Ebola outbreak (the curve is still rising); a new peace deal between Congo and Rwanda signed within seven days of the sanctions; the FATF grey-list removal being reversed; a volcanic eruption or major natural disaster in the east; Tshisekedi stepping down or being removed; a new Ebola vaccine being approved and rolled out nationally (the trial just started); the C64 opposition calling a successful general strike that shuts down Kinshasa for more than a day; a major oil or copper price shock that reshapes the fiscal conversation in one week.

The US sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry, the FATF grey-list removal, and the broader financial and diplomatic pressure make sanctions and international policy a central thread.
Kabila's emergence as a rebel leader, the FRN offensive threat around Uvira, the ADF insurgency, and the US-Rwanda-Congo military tangle make armed conflict and ground fighting the third major theme.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the Ebola outbreak grew from a serious but still-containable epidemic into the dominant story of the week and the second deadliest in history. Cases jumped from roughly 6,000 across eight provinces to over 10,000, deaths crossed 5,000, and the outbreak was confirmed outside Congo in Kenya and Nigeria with genome sequencing tying those cases to the Congolese chain. Uganda imposed a paid 21-day quarantine on returning citizens, the Central African Republic tightened border controls, and violence against health workers escalated to the point of a nurse being killed and a machete-wielding mob attacking responders. The vaccine trial that had just begun enrollment in the first photo is now described as a three-shot trial actively underway. The human stories of orphans and grieving families continued but took a back seat to the sheer scale of the numbers. The Kabila-M23/FRN axis grew from a newly formed alliance into a recognizable rebel leadership with a former president at its head. Tshisekedi publicly branded Kabila a 'supplétif,' a Brigadier General defected from the FARDC to the FRN, and tensions are building around Uvira with residents fearing a new offensive. This is a step up from the first photo, where the alliance was still in its organizing phase and the main tension was diplomatic (Belgium's 'incomprehensible and unacceptable' statement). A major new theme appeared: the United States imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry and the Zigama CSS bank for fueling the M23 conflict, a significant escalation that was not present in the first photo at all. Another new thread emerged linking gold smuggling through Uganda to the financing of the Islamic State-linked ADF insurgency, tying the mining sector, cross-border trade, and the insurgency into a single economic-military web. The artisanal mining sector saw its regulatory head suspended, and a Gates-backed company complained that China is frustrating exploration efforts, adding a China dimension that was absent before. On the positive side, the FATF removed DR Congo from its grey list, a small but meaningful financial credibility win. The opposition C64 platform met in Rome and rejected armed rebellion, while a controversial referendum law was adopted in parliament without their participation, sparking a legitimacy firestorm. Tshisekedi showed support for FIFA president Infantino in a soft-power gesture. Several themes from the first photo shrank or vanished entirely. The census obstacles in Kinshasa disappeared from the headlines completely; there is no mention of it in the second photo. The Glencore-Congo Mines deal, which was in 'final phases,' also vanished, suggesting it was either signed quietly or stalled. The Belgium-Kinshasa diplomatic rupture, which had been a standalone story with embassy communications being cut, faded into the broader Rwanda-Congo conflict narrative. The Hamilton-F1 moment and the Nigeria-Swiss Ebola case, which had been colorful international color pieces, were absorbed into the larger Ebola spread story and then dropped. The 'early gains faltering' framing of the outbreak was replaced by 'growing exponentially,' a much starker characterization. The overall motion is one of acceleration: the two dominant stories (Ebola and the Kabila-M23 conflict) both intensified, new economic and diplomatic threads (US-Rwanda sanctions, gold-ADF financing, mining regulation, FATF) appeared, and the secondary stories (census, mining deal, Belgium diplomacy, sports crossover) were either resolved, absorbed, or dropped. The conflict is becoming more legible as a civil war with a recognizable face rather than a faceless proxy war, and the economic underbelly that funds it is becoming visible.
delta.wind: The Ebola prediction was the strongest hit. The expectation was that cases would push toward 7,000 or higher, more international coverage of the vaccine trial would follow, at least one additional country might report a linked case, and the orphan and mental-health stories would continue. What actually happened exceeded the forecast: cases surpassed 10,000, not 7,000; deaths crossed 5,000, a number not specifically projected but implied by the trajectory; Kenya and Nigeria both confirmed cases with genome sequencing, exceeding the 'at least one additional country' bar; the three-shot vaccine trial is now actively underway rather than in its 'very first days of enrollment'; and the UN described the outbreak as growing exponentially, a starker framing than 'not contained.' The violence against health workers (a nurse killed, a machete mob) was not specifically predicted but fits naturally within the 'community mistrust' and 'human toll' themes. The expectation that the outbreak was 'not contained and the geographic spread makes containment within one week very unlikely' was exactly right. The Kabila-M23 prediction was directionally correct but underestimated the speed and form of escalation. The expectation was further Belgian statements, possible minor skirmishes, a Tshisekedi public address, and a 'real possibility of minor skirmishes or troop repositioning.' What happened was faster and more consequential: Kabila is now formally a rebel leader, not just an ally of M23; Tshisekedi called him a puppet; a Brigadier General defected; tensions are building around Uvira. The 'full-scale new offensive' was rated probable, and while we got tensions and repositioning rather than a full offensive, the formalization of Kabila's role is arguably a bigger step than a skirmish. The intra-government fracturing (arrest of a Tshisekedi party cadre) evolved into the referendum law adopted without opposition and the C64 meeting in Rome, which is a different but related form of political infighting. The census prediction was a miss in the sense that the story simply vanished. The expectation was that obstacles would persist and more reporting would follow. Instead, the census dropped out of the headlines entirely, suggesting either the TV5Monde coverage cluster was a one-day event or other stories crowded it out. The Glencore-Congo Mines deal prediction was also a miss in the sense of absence. The expectation was a possible official announcement or signing. Neither happened, and the story disappeared, leaving it unclear whether the deal was signed quietly or is still dragging. The international diplomatic reaction prediction was partially correct but under-specified. The expectation was a UN Security Council or AU statement, neighboring countries issuing diplomatic notes, and the Hamilton moment fading. The UN did describe the outbreak as exponential, and the Hamilton moment did fade. But the big diplomatic story was the US sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry and the Zigama CSS bank, which was not specifically predicted. The expectation mentioned 'neighboring countries watching closely,' but the US stepping in with sanctions on Rwanda's military machinery is a more consequential and different form of international reaction than what was anticipated. The 'less likely surprises' list was mostly right: no sudden ceasefire, no volcanic event, no second vaccine candidate showing early data. The 'second wave of arrests' evolved into the referendum law controversy rather than literal arrests. The 'things I would not bet on' list held up well: no coup, no Ebola containment, no full diplomatic break with Belgium (it faded rather than broke), no major European or American Ebola case, no census completion, no Kabila in Kinshasa, no oil or copper price shock. The main pattern of error in the expectations was over-weighting the two big stories (Ebola and Kabila-M23) and the secondary stories (census, mining deal) while under-weighting the broader economic-security web. The gold-ADF financing link, the artisanal mining crackdown, the China-exploration friction, the FATF grey list removal, and the US-Rwanda sanctions are all threads that connect the conflict to the economy in ways the first-photo expectations did not fully capture. The expectations treated the Kabila-M23 story as primarily a Congo-Belgium-Rwanda diplomatic drama, but the US sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry reframed it as a US-Rwanda-Congo trilateral with real financial teeth. The expectations also treated the mining sector as a separate 'economy' story (Glencore deal) rather than recognizing it as the funding mechanism for the ADF and the broader eastern conflict, which is where the gold smuggling, the regulatory suspension, and the China question all connect. The expectations were too focused on the political and health dimensions and not enough on the economic plumbing that sustains the conflict.
delta.driver: The force pushing DR Congo from the first photograph to the second is the convergence of exponential biological spread, formalized rebel leadership, and the economic plumbing that funds the conflict, all colliding in a week. The Ebola outbreak is not just a health event; it is a political and social stress test in a country where trust in institutions is already thin, and the violence against health workers, the paid quarantine Uganda imposed, and the village chief fighting prejudice all show a community under siege where the disease and the conflict feed each other. Simultaneously, the Kabila-M23/FRN axis crossed a threshold from a coalition of armed groups into a recognizable rebel leadership with a former president at its head, which changes how the conflict is perceived by both Congolese citizens and the international community, pulling the US into the picture with sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry and making the eastern conflict a trilateral US-Rwanda-Congo problem rather than a bilateral Congo-Rwanda one. Underneath both of these, the gold-smuggling-ADF-financing link and the artisanal mining crackdown reveal that the conflict is sustained by an economic circuit of illegal mining, cross-border trade, and insurgent taxation that the government is only now trying to tighten, and the FATF grey list removal and the China-exploration friction show that the country's financial credibility and its relationship with foreign capital are being renegotiated in real time. The referendum law adopted without opposition and the C64 meeting in Rome signal that the political stakes are rising as the conflict becomes more 'Congolese' and less 'proxy,' and the Tshisekedi-FIFA moment, however small, shows a government trying to project normalcy and soft power while the country is in crisis. The single underlying driver is that the conflict in eastern Congo has entered a phase where it can no longer be contained within a single bilateral relationship or a single sector; it is a health, military, economic, and political crisis all at once, and each week the threads pull tighter.

crystal.reasoning:
Starting from the present picture: the Ebola outbreak has crossed the 10,000-case and 5,000-death thresholds, making it the second deadliest in history, with confirmed spread to Kenya and Nigeria and a three-shot vaccine trial actively underway. The violence against health workers (a nurse killed, a machete mob) shows community trust is fracturing in real time. The Kabila-FRN axis has crossed a threshold: a former president is now the recognizable face of the armed opposition, a Brigadier General has defected, and tensions are building around Uvira. The US has moved from diplomatic observer to active sanctioning power, hitting Rwanda's defence ministry and the Zigama CSS bank. The gold-smuggling-ADF-financing link, the artisanal mining crackdown, and the China-exploration friction reveal an economic circuit that sustains the conflict. The FATF grey list removal is a small credibility win. The referendum law adopted without opposition and the C64 Rome meeting signal rising domestic political stakes. The Tshisekedi-FIFA moment is a soft-power gesture that will fade quickly.

Extending along the motion: The Ebola outbreak is in an exponential phase per the UN. The motion from 6,000 to 10,000 cases in roughly a week suggests the next week will see cases push toward 12,000-15,000 if the exponential curve holds, though it may begin to plateau in some provinces as treatment centres close (the one positive discharge story) while new provinces are hit. The international spread will likely add one or two more countries reporting linked cases or tightening borders. The vaccine trial will progress through enrollment, and early safety observations from the first cohort may be reported. The violence against health workers, now established as a pattern, is likely to produce at least one more incident in the coming week. Uganda's paid quarantine will generate complaints, disputes, and possibly a case slipping through the 21-day window. The Kabila-FRN axis will continue to formalize: more defectors, more rhetoric, and military repositioning around Uvira. A full-scale offensive within seven days is less likely than continued positioning and skirmish-level contact, but the motion makes a major engagement more probable than it looked a week ago. The US sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry will begin to show practical friction in procurement and banking, and Rwanda will likely issue a diplomatic response. The gold-ADF-mining web will generate more reporting as the Sentry report digests. The referendum law will generate more opposition friction, possibly protests or a formal C64 statement. The FATF win will be a brief mention, not a sustained story.

Correcting for the wind: Last time I over-weighted the two big stories (Ebola, Kabila-M23) and the secondary stories (census, Glencore deal) while under-weighting the economic-security web. The census and Glencore deal both vanished, confirming that secondary stories in Congo tend to disappear rather than develop. I should therefore not build the forecast around the Tshisekedi-FIFA moment or the Ash Dykes expedition; they will fade. I should weight the US-Rwanda-Congo trilateral dynamic more heavily, recognizing that the US is now a direct actor with financial teeth, not just a diplomatic voice. I should treat the mining sector as the funding mechanism for the conflict, not a separate economy story. I should be less conservative on Ebola numbers (last time I predicted 7,000 and got 10,000+) but acknowledge that exponential growth eventually meets logistical limits. I should not predict a sudden ceasefire, a coup, or Kabila in Kinshasa, as the 'things I would not bet on' list held up well last time. I should recognize that the C64's rejection of armed rebellion constrains the opposition from fully backing Kabila, which is a different dynamic than last time when the Kamerhe split was the main internal drama. The fracture is now inside Tshisekedi's own camp (the referendum law, the party cadre arrest), and that is where the next political pressure will build.

The single underlying driver for the coming week is the collision of three accelerating processes in the same geographic space: an exponentially spreading virus in eastern Congo, a formalizing rebel leadership with a former president at its head, and an economic circuit of gold, smuggling, and foreign capital that funds the conflict and is now being targeted by US sanctions. Each of these pulls the others tighter. The government in Kinshasa must manage all three simultaneously while its own ruling coalition shows cracks over the referendum law. The international community, led by the US, is moving from watching to intervening, but the interventions (sanctions on Rwanda's military, not Congo's) suggest a strategy of pressuring the patron rather than the principal, which will keep the conflict simmering rather than resolving it.
crystal.forecast:
THE EBOLA OUTBREAK REMAINS THE DOMINANT STORY AND CONTINUES TO ACCELERATE. Cases will likely push past 12,000 and possibly toward 15,000 as the exponential curve continues in North Kivu and surrounding provinces, though the closure of one treatment centre and the discharge of its last patients suggest some local pockets are stabilizing while the overall picture worsens. Deaths will likely cross 6,000. At least one additional country, possibly two, will report a linked case or tighten border controls in response to the Kenya and Nigeria confirmations. Uganda's paid 21-day quarantine will generate visible friction: complaints from returning citizens, at least one dispute over who pays, and a small chance of a case slipping through the quarantine window. The three-shot vaccine trial will continue enrollment, and early safety observations from the first vaccinated cohort may be reported by the trial's sponsors or the WHO. Violence against health workers is likely to produce at least one more incident, given the established pattern of a nurse killed and a machete mob attacking responders; community mistrust in the eastern provinces is deep enough that a second or third attack on a health team is more probable than not. The UN and WHO will likely issue updated guidance or a coordination statement, and the outbreak's designation as the second deadliest in history will anchor every major wire service's Africa desk. Confidence: HIGH that Ebola remains the single most-covered story; MEDIUM on the specific case and death numbers, as exponential growth eventually meets logistical and geographic limits.

THE KABILA-FRN CONFLICT FORMS INTO A RECOGNIZABLE CIVIL WAR WITH A FACE. Kabila's formal role as rebel leader will generate more rhetoric from both sides: Tshisekedi's camp will continue to brand him a puppet of Rwanda, while Kabila's supporters will emphasize his national legitimacy. The Brigadier General Kamanzi defection will likely be followed by one or two more mid-level FARDC officers joining the FRN, as the formalization of the rebel structure makes defection more attractive. Tensions around Uvira will escalate: residents are already fearing a new offensive, and the military repositioning that has been building will likely produce skirmish-level contact or a minor engagement, though a full-scale FRN offensive within seven days is less likely than continued positioning and probing. The C64's rejection of armed rebellion in Rome constrains the opposition from fully backing Kabila, which means the conflict will remain a Kabila-Rwanda axis against Tshisekedi rather than a broad national opposition war, but the C64 will likely issue a follow-up statement or protest about the referendum law adopted without their participation, adding a domestic political layer to the military one. Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH that the conflict intensifies in rhetoric and repositioning; MEDIUM on whether a major engagement occurs; LOW on a full-scale offensive.

US SANCTIONS ON RWANDA'S DEFENCE MINISTRY BEGIN TO SHOW PRACTICAL EFFECTS AND DRAW A KIGALI RESPONSE. The sanctions on the defence ministry and the Zigama CSS bank will create friction in Rwanda's military procurement and banking over the coming week. Rwanda is likely to issue a diplomatic statement, possibly through its foreign ministry or the president's office, expressing concern or frustration while stopping short of a formal break. The US may follow up with a statement clarifying that the sanctions target military machinery, not the civilian government, reinforcing the deliberate-signal character of the move. There is a moderate chance of US-Rwanda back-channel talks or a phone call between the two foreign ministries, though a formal summit is less likely within a week. The sanctions will also complicate Rwanda's ability to sustain M23/FRN logistics, which may slow the pace of the eastern conflict slightly, though the effect will be felt more over months than days. Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH that Rwanda responds diplomatically; MEDIUM on the practical friction becoming visible in reporting; LOW on a formal US-Rwanda summit.

THE GOLD-ADF-MINING ECONOMIC WEB GENERATES MORE REPORTING AND POLICY RESPONSE. The Sentry report linking gold smuggling through Uganda to ADF financing will be digested by policymakers and journalists over the coming week, generating at least one or two follow-up pieces that connect the dots between the artisanal mining crackdown, the ADF insurgency, and the cross-border trade routes. The suspension of the artisanal mining regulatory head will likely be followed by either a replacement appointment or a parliamentary question, and the government may announce a short-term inspection or crackdown in the eastern mining zones. The China-exploration friction, as reported by the Gates-backed company, will generate a smaller but notable piece on the Congo-China economic relationship, possibly with a Chinese ministry or state-owned enterprise response. The ADF may carry out at least one attack in a gold mining area, reinforcing the economic-military link in the public eye. Confidence: MEDIUM that this thread generates more headlines; MEDIUM-HIGH that the ADF carries out an attack in a mining zone.

DOMESTIC POLITICS: THE REFERENDUM LAW AND THE C64 FRICTION. The referendum law adopted without opposition participation will continue to generate friction. The C64, having met in Rome and rejected armed rebellion, is likely to issue a formal statement or hold a press conference in Kinshasa protesting the law's legitimacy, possibly calling for a parliamentary review or a constitutional court challenge. Tshisekedi's camp will defend the law as necessary for the country's future, and the intra-party dynamics (the earlier arrest of a cadre calling for weapons) will keep the ruling coalition's unity under a low-level spotlight. The Tshisekedi-FIFA-Infantino moment will fade quickly, as last week's census and Glencore stories did, and will not generate more than a brief mention. Confidence: MEDIUM that the referendum law generates a C64 protest or statement; LOW that it is repealed or sent to the constitutional court within the week.

WHAT I WOULD NOT BET ON: A sudden ceasefire between Congo and Rwanda. Ebola being contained or a miracle treatment emerging. A coup or major military takeover in Kinshasa. Kabila physically entering Kinshasa. The referendum law being repealed. A full-scale FRN offensive with a major territorial gain. The FATF grey list removal generating more than a brief positive mention. A volcanic eruption or major natural disaster. The Ash Dykes expedition generating a second wave of coverage. A major European or American Ebola case (though the Kenya and Nigeria cases make a further jump more plausible than a week ago, a case in London or New York within seven days is still a stretch).

crystal.eli5:
The big story in the Democratic Republic of Congo right now is an Ebola outbreak that has gotten really, really bad. More than 10,000 people have been sick and more than 5,000 have died. That makes it the second worst Ebola outbreak ever. The virus has already jumped to Kenya and Nigeria, and more countries are closing their borders or making people who come back from Congo sit in quarantine for three weeks. A new vaccine is being tested, and that is a good sign, but the outbreak is still growing fast. In the next week, expect the numbers to keep climbing, more countries to report cases or tighten their borders, and probably another incident where health workers get attacked by angry communities who are scared and mistrustful.

The second big story is a kind of civil war in the eastern part of the country. A former president named Joseph Kabila has become the leader of a rebel group called the FRN, and he is fighting against the current president, Tshisekedi. A high-ranking general has left the national army to join Kabila's side. People in the town of Uvira are worried that a new military push is coming. The United States just put sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry because it is helping the rebels, which is a big deal. Expect more arguments and posturing from all sides, and probably some small fights or troop movements, but not a full-blown battle in the next seven days.

Underneath all of this is a money story that is easy to miss. Gold is being smuggled out of Congo through Uganda, and that money is paying for the weapons of an Islamic State-linked rebel group called the ADF. The government just fired the head of its mining regulator because of illegal activity, and a company backed by Bill Gates says China is making it hard to explore for minerals. The good news is that an international group called the FATF removed Congo from its grey list, which means banks and businesses will have a little less paperwork to deal with. But the money that flows through gold and copper is what keeps the wars going, and that is the thread connecting everything.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A correctly identified the dominant themes: Ebola as the central story with rising cases, international spread, vaccine trial coverage, and the Kabila-M23 axis as the political-military story. It got the direction of the Ebola outbreak right (rising, spreading internationally, North Kivu as epicenter) but underestimated the magnitude, predicting 7,000-8,000 cases when the actual total passed 10,000. The prediction of at least one more country joining the affected list was correct (Kenya and Nigeria confirmed via genome sequencing). The vaccine trial generating steady reporting was accurate. The mental-health and human-toll angle was partially validated by the AP village-chief feature. The Tshisekedi party-drama prediction (second arrest, factional statement, public address) was loosely validated by the referendum-law controversy and the C64 Rome meeting, though the specific 'distribute weapons' rhetoric angle was less prominent than expected. The Belgium-DRC diplomatic maneuvering prediction (ambassador recall, back-channel dialogue) was fairly specific and did not clearly materialize in the week's headlines; Belgium was a background presence rather than a headline actor. The Glencore deal prediction was the most notable miss: A rated it moderate-high confidence for announcement or major update, yet the deal did not appear in any headline. The census prediction (continued coverage, government response, secondary status) was reasonable, though the story faded more than A anticipated. The Hamilton-fading prediction was correct. What A missed entirely: the US sanctions on Rwanda's defense ministry and Zigama CSS bank (a major, multi-outlet story), the gold-smuggling/ADF financial link, the FATF grey-list removal (a positive headline), the violence against health workers (nurse killed, mob attack), Uganda's 21-day quarantine, the artisanal-mining crackdown, and the Tshisekedi-FIFA soft-power play. A's overall picture was directionally correct on the big two stories (Ebola, Kabila-M23) but overconfident on the Glencore and Belgium items, and blind to the Rwanda sanctions, which was arguably the week's second-biggest story.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B correctly identified Ebola as the dominant and widening story, the Kabila-M23 alliance as the central political thread, the census as a fading secondary story, and the Glencore deal as uncertain. Its Ebola prediction was directionally right but also underestimated the caseload ('push toward 7,000 or higher' versus the actual 10,000+). The international-spread prediction (Kenya, Nigeria) was correct. The vaccine-trial timing (first days of enrollment, no results) was accurate. The Kabila-M23 section correctly framed the alliance as the central story and anticipated Tshisekedi framing the crisis as an external threat, which was validated by his 'supplétif' remark. The prediction of minor skirmishes or troop repositioning was roughly correct given the Uvira tensions and Kamanzi's defection to the FRN. However, B rated a full-scale new offensive as 'probable,' which was slightly too optimistic since no such offensive materialized. The Belgium-diplomacy prediction was similar to A's and also less prominent than expected. The Glencore call was the key differentiator: B explicitly hedged, saying 'possible rather than probable' and noting that 'final phases can drag.' The deal was not announced, so B's caution was the better read. The census prediction (tapering coverage, not resolving) was correct. The international-diplomacy section (UN/AU statement, neighboring-country reactions) was partially validated by Uganda's quarantine and the general regional attention, though a formal UNSC or AU emergency session did not clearly appear in the headlines. B's 'less likely surprises' list was well-calibrated: the ceasefire, second wave of arrests, volcanic event, Glencore signing, and early vaccine data all did not materialize. The 'things I would not bet on' list was entirely correct: no coup, no containment, no full Belgium break, no European Ebola case, no census completion, no Kabila in Kinshasa, no copper price shock. What B missed: the US sanctions on Rwanda (a major story), the gold/ADF financial link, the FATF removal, the referendum-law controversy (though 'political infighting' is adjacent), the health-worker violence, the Tshisekedi-FIFA angle, and the artisanal-mining crackdown. B's overall picture was directionally sound, its probability labels were better calibrated than A's, and its explicit 'I would not bet on' list gave a reader a clear sense of what was unlikely, all of which proved accurate.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts captured the two dominant stories (Ebola and Kabila-M23) in the right direction and correctly identified the vaccine trial, the international spread, the census as secondary, and the Hamilton moment as fading. Both underestimated the Ebola caseload magnitude. Both missed the US sanctions on Rwanda, which was the week's most significant non-Ebola story, as well as the gold/ADF link, the FATF removal, the health-worker violence, and the referendum-law controversy. The key differentiator is calibration. Forecast A made more confident, specific predictions that did not fully materialize: the Glencore deal 'likely to be announced' (moderate-high confidence) when it was not announced at all; the Belgium ambassador recall or back-channel dialogue as a near-certainty when Belgium was a background presence; and the 'non-traveler transmission pattern' as a specific narrative thread that was less prominent than the straightforward Kenya-Nigeria confirmations. Forecast B, by contrast, explicitly hedged on Glencore ('possible rather than probable'), rated the full-scale offensive as 'probable' rather than near-certain (and was closer to the truth), and provided a 'things I would not bet on' list that was 100% accurate. B's probability framework (almost certain, probable, possible) gave a reader a more actionable and honest picture of what to expect. A's structure was more detailed and its human-toll and clinical-trial angles were slightly sharper, but the extra specificity came at the cost of overconfidence. For a reader trying to prepare for the week ahead, B's more measured tone, correct hedging on the uncertain items, and clean list of what was unlikely would have served better. Neither forecast was wrong in its big-picture read, but B's calibrations were more reliable.
